subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If the coefficients of the r-th, (r + 1)-th and (r + 2)-th terms in the expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ are in A.P., then show that n² − (4r + 1)n + 4r² − 2 = 0.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — what the three coefficients are, what being in A.P. means once you divide by the middle one, the two ratio formulas you substitute, and how the algebra reaches n² − (4r + 1)n + 4r² − 2 = 0.
insider_note: The r-th TERM's coefficient is ⁿCᵣ₋₁, not ⁿCᵣ — the index runs one behind the position. Start one index low or every later line proves a different equation from the one printed.

steps.label: Name the three coefficients
steps.margin_note: First mark. The r-th term is Tᵣ = ⁿCᵣ₋₁ xʳ⁻¹, so the three coefficients are ⁿCᵣ₋₁, ⁿCᵣ, ⁿCᵣ₊₁ — the index runs one behind the position.

recall.must_convey: That the coefficients of the r-th, (r + 1)-th, (r + 2)-th terms are ⁿCᵣ₋₁, ⁿCᵣ, ⁿCᵣ₊₁.

steps.why: A coefficient of (1 + x)ⁿ is a binomial coefficient, and the coefficient of the r-th term carries r − 1, not r. Naming the three correctly is the step the rest of the answer depends on.
common_mistakes: Taking the r-th term's coefficient as ⁿCᵣ — it is ⁿCᵣ₋₁.
Writing the three coefficients as ⁿCᵣ, ⁿCᵣ₊₁, ⁿCᵣ₊₂, which proves a different equation.

steps.label: Write the A.P. condition
steps.margin_note: Three numbers are in A.P. when the middle one is the average of the other two: 2·(middle) = (first) + (last). Divide through by the middle coefficient so the ratios appear.

recall.must_convey: That 2·ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCᵣ₋₁ + ⁿCᵣ₊₁, and dividing by ⁿCᵣ gives 2 = ⁿCᵣ₋₁/ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₊₁/ⁿCᵣ.
accept: twice n C r equals n C r minus one plus n C r plus one, divide by n C r to get two equals the sum of the two ratios
A P means two times the middle equals the sum of the ends, then divide by the middle
two equals n C r minus one by n C r plus n C r plus one by n C r
A P condition rasi n C r tho divide cheste two equals two ratios
middle coefficient is the average of the other two

steps.why: Dividing by the middle coefficient turns three binomial coefficients into two RATIOS of consecutive coefficients, and those ratios have a one-line formula.
common_mistakes: Writing the A.P. condition as first + middle = last.
Not dividing by the middle term and trying to expand the factorials.

steps.label: Replace the ratios
steps.margin_note: Third and fourth marks. ⁿCᵣ₋₁/ⁿCᵣ = r/(n − r + 1) and ⁿCᵣ₊₁/ⁿCᵣ = (n − r)/(r + 1).

recall.must_convey: That the two ratios are r/(n − r + 1) and (n − r)/(r + 1), so 2 = r/(n − r + 1) + (n − r)/(r + 1).
accept: n C r minus one by n C r is r by n minus r plus one and n C r plus one by n C r is n minus r by r plus one

steps.why: ⁿCᵣ/ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = (n − r + 1)/r and ⁿCᵣ₊₁/ⁿCᵣ = (n − r)/(r + 1) come straight from the factorial form; they replace every binomial coefficient by plain algebra in n and r.
common_mistakes: Inverting one of the two ratios.
Using (n − r)/r instead of (n − r + 1)/r for the lower ratio.

steps.label: Clear fractions and simplify
steps.margin_note: Fifth to seventh marks. Multiply out both sides fully before collecting — the r² terms cancel on one side and the n² term appears on the other.
lines: 2(nr + n − r² + 1) = r² + r + n² − 2nr + r² + n − r

recall.must_convey: That cross-multiplying gives 2(n − r + 1)(r + 1) = r(r + 1) + (n − r)(n − r + 1), and collecting terms gives n² − (4r + 1)n + 4r² − 2 = 0.

expanding and collecting gives n squared minus four r plus one n plus four r squared minus two equals zero

steps.why: Cross-multiplying once and collecting like terms is all that remains; the required equation is exactly what falls out, with nothing to guess.
common_mistakes: Expanding (n − r)(n − r + 1) as n² − r² + n − r.
Losing the −2 that comes from 2·1 on the left.
